chemicals.concentration_notes: ◦ Severity: The toxicity is classified as Moderate. ◦ Dose-Dependent Effects: While oral irritation is the primary sign, ingesting larger quantities can lead to more systemic issues such as diarrhea and lethargy.
chemicals.description: ◦ Physical Irritation: When the plant is chewed, it releases needle-like crystals that cause immediate and painful irritation to the sensitive tissues of the mouth, tongue, and throat. This results in symptoms such as intense burning, excessive drooling, and difficulty swallowing.
chemicals.name: Insoluble calcium oxalate crystals

description:
Homalomena ‘Selby’ is a tropical houseplant in the Araceae family. Like pothos, philodendron, and dieffenbachia, it is unsafe for cats because the leaves and stems contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals.

When a cat bites the plant, the crystals can press into the mouth and throat like tiny needles. This causes fast pain and burning. The plant’s sap may add more irritation, especially on the lips, tongue, or throat.

A cat may drool, paw at the mouth, vomit, or have swelling of the lips or tongue. Most cats stop chewing quickly because it hurts, but swelling can still be serious. Keep Homalomena out of reach, rinse the mouth gently with water if safe, and call a veterinarian if swelling, vomiting, or breathing trouble appears.
name: Homalomena Selby / Homalomena rubescens
safetyNotes: Toxic compounds: insoluble calcium oxalate raphides; the plant’s cell sap also contains proteolytic enzymes
Mechanism: crystal penetration of the mouth and throat lining causes mechanical burning and inflammation
Symptoms: sudden oral pain, intense drooling, pawing at mouth, swollen lips or tongue, difficulty swallowing, vomiting
All parts of the plant are hazardous; the reaction is immediate and self-limiting
Rinse the mouth with water; seek veterinary care if swallowing is impaired or symptoms do not resolve

symptoms.name: Mouth Irritation (Pain/Burning)
symptoms.notes: The needle-like crystals embed in the soft tissues of the mouth and tongue, causing immediate discomfort.

symptoms.name: Drooling (Hypersalivation)
symptoms.notes: This is a direct reaction to the pain and irritation caused by the crystals in the mouth.

symptoms.name: Vomiting
symptoms.notes: Occurs as the body attempts to expel the irritating plant material.Reluctance to Eat (Anorexia)

symptoms.name: Reluctance to Eat / Difficulty Swallowing
symptoms.notes: The cat may refuse food due to the pain and swelling in the mouth and throat.

symptoms.name: Diarrhea
symptoms.notes: This symptom is noted specifically if the plant is "ingested in quantity."

symptoms.name: Lethargy
symptoms.notes: Like diarrhea, this is more likely to occur if a significant amount of the plant has been consumed.

treatments.description: The veterinarian (or owner, under guidance) flushes the cat's mouth thoroughly with water. This helps to mechanically remove the needle-like oxalate crystals (raphides) and plant material that are embedding in the oral mucosa and causing pain.
treatments.name: Oral Rinsing / Irrigation
treatments.notes: This is the primary and most immediate step to relieve the intense burning and irritation caused by the crystals. It effectively reduces the source of the pain.Administration of Demulcents (Calcium Binding)

treatments.description: The cat is fed or administered milk, yogurt, or another calcium-containing liquid. The calcium in these products binds to the insoluble oxalate crystals, helping to neutralize them and facilitate their clearance from the mouth and esophagus.
treatments.name: Administration of Dairy Products (Milk or Yogurt)
treatments.notes: This can soothe the irritated tissues and is often recommended alongside rinsing to provide relief from the "pins and needles" sensation.

treatments.description: ◦ Fluids: Intravenous (IV) or subcutaneous fluids are administered to correct dehydration if the cat has been vomiting or refusing to drink due to mouth pain. ◦ Medications: Anti-emetics (to stop vomiting) and analgesics (pain relievers) may be given to manage gastrointestinal distress and oral discomfort.
treatments.name: Fluid Therapy, Anti-emetics, and Analgesics
treatments.notes: This is necessary if the cat is experiencing persistent vomiting, diarrhea, or is lethargic and unable to eat. Most animals recover within 24–48 hours with this supportive care.Airway Management (Rare)

treatments.description: In rare, severe cases where laryngeal edema (swelling of the throat) occurs, the veterinarian may need to provide supplemental oxygen or secure the airway (intubation) to ensure the cat can breathe.
treatments.name: Oxygen Support and Airway Security
treatments.notes: While swelling is a common symptom of insoluble oxalate ingestion, severe respiratory distress is less common but requires immediate emergency intervention if it occurs.
